#10633. Before you trust consultants’ ‘research,’ look for these red flags

When Enron, which Fortune named “America’s Most Innovative Company” for six consecutive years, collapsed in 2001, there was no shortage of blame to go around. Many blamed corruption and greed, others hubris, and still others incompetence. But Nobel laureate Paul Krugman offered a different explanation.

In his New York Times column, Death By Guru, he identified the culprit as trendy management theories. He argued, essentially, that consultants selling compelling narratives persuade gullible CEOs to abandon fact-based analysis and good sense. Inevitably, reality catches up, and there is a price to be paid.

Yet there is a deeper problem. When a big consulting company sells a story, it’s not merely giving advice, but presenting its assertions as being backed by “research.” When they use the term, however, they rarely, if ever, mean that they have used the scientific method and employed appropriate controls for error and bias. These are the tricks of the trade. 

1. The Case Study

Organizations are often inscrutable and hard to research. That’s why consultants tend to rely heavily on case study interviews. These purport to leverage consultants’ rare access to insiders in order to glean insight others cannot. These can sometimes be helpful, but they also have severe limitations that are often overlooked. 

First, with shareholders and customers to please, managers are seldom eager to talk about failures. So we usually only hear about successes. Those, of course, are important but also subject to survivorship bias. For example, if a risky strategy results in 1% of the firms being wildly successful and 99% going out of business, then we’ll tend to hear glowing accounts of that lucky 1% and we’ll miss the vast majority that flamed out.

Another issue with the case study method is that it is necessarily limited. When researchers conducted a case study on a company I used to run, to take just one example, they interviewed insiders (including me) and did their best to interpret what they heard and what they could glean from background information about the market.

While I don’t think anything was inaccurate, it didn’t capture the reality either. Only a handful of people were interviewed, almost all of them from a single part of the business, and none of them, besides me, were involved in making decisions. The issues presented in the case study simply weren’t the ones we were actually wrestling with.

Finally, case studies rarely offer much in the way of documentation. In more rigorous fields like, say, sociology or psychology, researchers are expected to share their methods and data so that others can interpret them. Unfortunately, that’s rarely true in consulting research.

2. The Industry Survey

Besides case studies, another common technique for analyzing business trends and performance is the executive survey. Typically, a research company or consulting firm sends out questionnaires to executives. It then publishes a report with findings like 57% of companies are in the emerging stage of digital transformation and 49% of C-suite executives plan to diversify their supply chains.

This appearance of scientific rigor is largely a mirage. Yes, there are numbers, graphs, and pie charts, much as you would see in a scientific paper, but important information is often missing, such as how respondents were selected, how questions were phrased, how representative the sample was, and how the answers were interpreted.

Another problem is that these types of studies emphasize what a typical executive thinks about a particular business issue or trend. So what they really measure is the current zeitgeist, which may or may not reflect market reality. A great business strategy does not merely reflect what typical executives know, but exploits what they do not.

Perhaps most importantly, these types of surveys are generally not marketed as simple opinion surveys, but as sources of profound insight designed to help leaders gain an edge over their competitors. The numbers, graphs, and pie charts are specifically designed to look “scientific” in order to make them appear to be statements of empirical fact.

Surveys can tell you what executives think. They cannot tell you whether those executives are right or even well informed. As the mathematician G.H. Hardy once put it, “It is never worth a first-class man’s time to express a majority opinion. By definition, there are plenty of others to do that.”

3. The Industry Conference

A third weapon that consulting firms have in their arsenal is the industry conference, in which “industry experts” appear to speak along with the firm’s in-house gurus. The idea is that participants will get the opportunity to learn about the latest research and trends to help them make better decisions and get ahead of the competition. 

Yet what is the nature of the expertise being presented? Often, the executives who provide case study interviews and respond to industry surveys are the same people who appear onstage and sit in the audience. Essentially, consulting firms are selling their clients’ ideas back to them.

So while these conferences are touted as promoting “out-of-the-box thinking,” what they really do is create echo chambers for the narratives that the consulting firm is already pushing. Executives are wined and dined. A consensus is forged, and ideas that don’t conform are subtly discredited in favor of the officially backed zeitgeist. 

That doesn’t mean the ideas are bad, necessarily. And consultants often do outstanding work that benefits their clients. Yet it is also a salient fact that consulting firms have been behind the strategies involved in many major business scandals, whether it’s Enron, Purdue Pharma’s promotion of opioids, or Allstate’s questionable efforts to lowball claims.

It’s a simple truth that consultants’ main focus is on making their clients happy. Sometimes that means telling hard truths, and sometimes that means telling them what they want to hear. 

Don’t believe everything you think

In Richard Feynman’s 1974 commencement speech at the California Institute of Technoloy, or Caltech, he recounted going to a new-age resort where people were learning reflexology. A man was sitting in a hot tub rubbing a woman’s big toe and asking the instructor, “Is this the pituitary?” Unable to contain himself, the great physicist blurted out, “You’re a hell of a long way from the pituitary, man!”

His point was that it’s relatively easy to make something appear “scientific” by, for example, presenting data in official-looking charts and tables, but that doesn’t really make it science. Consultants often boast that their “research” consists of hundreds of case study interviews and large databases containing data on thousands of firms. But without the proper methods and controls, those things are meaningless.

Another problem: While many top-tier consultants have blue-chip résumés coming from top schools, very few have had experience operating a business. Often they’re people who’ve been told they’re smart all their lives, have never failed, and expect others to be impressed by their ideas, not to examine them thoroughly.

The truth is that the world is a messy place. Many of the most important assets, like relationships and trust, don’t fit neatly into Excel spreadsheets. Ideas can only be validated forward, never backward. There are countless ways a seemingly sound, logical idea can fail in the marketplace.

So take ideas that are purported to be “scientifically backed” or “research-based” with a grain of salt. An idea is just an idea. The marketplace will tell you if it’s a good one or not.

#10630. Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain

Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an important role in how computers store and process data.

A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.

Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).

Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.

"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.

Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers

The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.

One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.

"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.

Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.

Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.

The latest research represents an important advance toward that goal.

Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time

Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.

Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.

In the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.

"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.

The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.

A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing

Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.

The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.

"The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.

Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.

By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.

"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.

#10629. No one knows how to dress for work anymore—even executives

Companies spent years dragging employees back to the office, but forgot to tell them what to wear. The result is confusion stretching from junior employees to the executive suite.

One of Grant Alexander’s longtime clients is the COO of a big private company. He recently lamented that a few of his vice presidents had asked him what they should wear to an event.

“He looked at me, and he’s like, ‘When was the last time a VP had to ask the COO what they should be wearing for something?’” Alexander, the founder of Grant Alexander Studio, an executive image and styling consultancy, tells Fast Company. “A lot of the executives I work with have never talked to their employees about this.” 

When the COVID-19 pandemic began, people still wore their office attire for the first few weeks. But as the lockdowns went on, smart trousers were replaced with sweatpants, and shirts were put away to make room for T-shirts and hoodies.

“Now there’s a gap between what people believe they should be wearing at the office, and what their wardrobe actually has become,” says Alexander. “So they’re just like, ‘I don’t know what I should be wearing right now’.”

The uncertainty is far reaching. A 2025 survey of 1,000 hybrid workers in the U.S. by International Workplace Group (IWG) found that workers reported feeling stressed or anxious about what to wear to the office around seven times a month. Almost half (46%) said this happened at least weekly, while 14% experienced it daily. 

Zoom dressing is no longer an option

Samantha Harman, a former newspaper editor turned personal stylist, tells Fast Company that knowing what to wear to the office has always been complicated. But return to office (RTO) has made it even harder, with so much ambiguity around what’s expected. 

For people whose work wardrobes have been neglected for the past few years, remembering and updating their personal style can be a daunting prospect.

“I am working with quite a few people who’ve got return to office mandates for the New Year, and they’re now looking at their wardrobe thinking, ‘I couldn’t go into the office like this’,” Harman says. “It’s all very well ‘top dressing,’ or Zoom dressing—where you are presenting yourself in a certain way on screen, but on the bottom you’ve got your pajamas on. But you can’t do that face-to-face.”

In one recent conversation, a manager told Harman that people either came to the office looking like they’d just rolled out of bed, or were so put together they could have been going to the opera. When she asked if he’d spoken to them about it, he replied: “Are you kidding? I don’t even know what the rules or the guidelines are.”

The problem is compounded by the fact that workplace dress codes haven’t always kept pace with changing expectations, Harman says. Companies continue to rely on generic terms such as “business casual” without explaining what they mean in practice. 

The confusion also can add to workers’ mental load. Harman recently overheard two men debating whether or not an invitation specifying “smart casual” meant they needed to wear a tie. “You’re giving your employees more work to do,” she says.

Clarity is particularly important for juniors

Francesca O’Connor, cofounder of the workplace culture, leadership, and communications consultancy HappyHQ, tells Fast Company that leaders need to explain what dressing appropriately actually means for their specific organization. They also must distinguish between expectations for an ordinary office day and something that requires stepping it up, such as a client pitch.

“That doesn’t mean everyone needs to wear a suit,” she says. “It means having the judgment to understand your audience and what the situation calls for.”

This is particularly important for younger workers entering the office for the first time, who may have had little opportunity to observe traditional workplace style.

“If there’s an expectation that people dress differently for certain occasions, explain it,” O’Connor says. “Don’t leave them guessing, particularly when they’re starting out in their careers.”

In the IWG survey, 94% of Gen Z respondents said they wanted guidance on what to wear to work, compared with 84% of millennials, 70% of Gen X and 61% of baby boomers. 

“Gen Z entering the workforce have no idea what to wear and nobody’s talking about it,” Alexander says. “So they’re just like, ‘OK, I have joggers. I’m just going to wear them.’ And it usually takes them getting yelled at and something happening and somebody correcting them.”

Guidelines can help build confidence

Beyond avoiding awkward conversations, clearer expectations could help employees feel more confident at work, Harman says. 

“If you are wearing something that makes you feel really good, you will behave in a different way than if you’re wearing something that makes you feel a bit like a potato,” she says.

The best way for leaders to have this conversation with their employees is to get their buy-in, Harman adds, by asking what they actually love to wear and what makes them feel confident.

“Even if you just host some workshops or forums where you have people talking about this stuff, [it] can be really helpful,” Harman says. “People often tell me, ‘this is not ever something that we ever speak about at work, and yet it affects me every single day—because every single day, the one thing that I have to do is get dressed’.”

Alexander believes that focusing heavily on getting people back to the office without considering how they present themselves is shortsighted. It’s also easily fixed, he says, with a simple email or Slack update.

“You can say, ‘Hey, a few people have asked us lately about what we should wear.’ Nobody’s going to question it,” he says. “Executives can make it easier on the entire organization by just talking about it.”

That’s if the executives themselves know what protocol should be, of course.

#10627. This Googlebook is driving me crazy

Right now, Googlebooks make more sense for Google than they do for users.

After trying for years to bring Android features to Chromebooks, Google decided to start over with Android as the foundation for a new laptop operating system. The first wave of Googlebooks are high-end laptops (priced $900 and up), with Google pitching them as the ultimate computers for Android enthusiasts.

But in their current form, Googlebooks are a disjointed mess, with websites and apps that don’t work quite right and AI features that aren’t fully fleshed out. While having a single operating system and app platform across laptops and mobile devices might make life easier for Google, it doesn’t yet translate to a better experience than the Chromebooks that Google aims to replace.

Android’s not ready for laptops

For the past month I’ve been using Acer’s Googlebook 14, which is the cheapest Googlebook at $900, and the only one whose touchscreen flips around into tablet mode. I have no major complaints about the hardware, which has a featherweight 2.51-pound chassis, a rich 120 Hz 3K OLED screen, and a smooth trackpad (albeit a “diving board” type whose click mechanism stiffens at the top edge).

My frustrations are more on the software side, where Android isn’t ready to carry a real laptop workload.

While Google is pushing developers to optimize their Android apps for large screens, keyboards, and trackpads, Google itself hasn’t always bothered to do so. The preloaded version of Gmail, for instance, is not an optimized Android app, but rather a web-based desktop app powered by the Chrome browser. Same goes for Google Docs, Drive, Meet, and YouTube. Tapping the menu button in these apps reveals a “Running in Chrome” disclaimer, and any Chrome extensions you install will apply to these apps as well.

This wouldn’t be a major concern if the web apps worked the way they’re supposed to. In Gmail, though, cursor hover controls don’t work, so you can’t quickly trash or archive messages line by line in the inbox. In Google Drive, documents open in a Chrome browser tab, while the same documents open in their own windows via Google Docs or Sheets. And if you try to select text in Google Docs using the touchscreen, the comment button pops up directly over the right text selector, making it unreachable.

Third-party Android apps can also have issues. Signing into Slack bounces me out to a Chrome tab, which then fails to authenticate back inside the Android app, so the only way to gain access is by manually entering a URL and password for each workplace. Even then, Slack’s Android app is poorly optimized, without the desktop version’s persistent sidebar.

Video apps still feel unfinished on Googlebooks as well. Those that Google deems “optimized for desktop,” such as Netflix and Disney+, will automatically open in full screen, which is jarring but at least fits the use case of watching video. Others, such as Fox One and NFL, open in a floating desktop window, and clicking their full screen icons accomplishes nothing. You’re actually supposed to ignore that button, highlight the maximize button in the window controls, then click the little “Full Screen” icon. Optimized or not, none of these apps support always-visible picture-in-picture mode like their mobile counterparts.

One last nitpick, admittedly a niche one: Bookmarklets don’t work on Googlebooks. I keep more than dozen of these in my browser’s address bar, which allows me to launch site-specific searches, create page excerpts, find archived versions of web pages, and remove “sticky” page elements. Not being able to use them on the Googlebook is a reminder that you’re not quite getting a full Chrome desktop experience.

The app situation will likely improve over time. When I started using the Googlebook, it wouldn’t let me install the Bluesky app and directed me to the web version. Now the app is available. Google Docs has also gained the ability to mark individual documents for offline use, which wasn’t possible at the outset. The Google Play Store has a tiered labeling system—“Optimized for Desktop,” “Compatible with Desktop,” “Better on the Website”—so you know what to expect, but for now the ecosystem is a work in progress.

Android synergies in progress

Googlebooks do have some neat features for Android users, the best of which is being able to access your phone’s files directly through the laptop’s Files app. There’s also “cross-device continuity,” which doesn’t work with many apps, but lets you quickly continue editing a message in Gmail or a document in Google Docs after opening it up on your phone.

App casting is rougher. If you have a phone running Android 17, this lets you view your phone’s apps through a Googlebook without installing them, and while this might be useful in some scenarios, it’s a subpar experience with jerky scrolling and occasional formatting issues. It can also lead to annoyances, like when a phone notification pops up on the Googlebook, and tapping it takes you into the janky app-casting version instead of the one that’s installed on your computer.

Android as a desktop operating system will also inherently pose some limitations. AI apps like ChatGPT and Claude lack the device control and folder-based file permissions that their desktop apps offer, and there are no command bar apps akin to Raycast for Windows and MacOS. The relative simplicity of an Android-based laptop may be a positive for some, but for me it’s a hindrance.

Too many Geminis

Beyond just catering to Android enthusiasts, Google is pitching Googlebooks as a premier surface for its Gemini AI assistant. In practice this means there are four main ways to invoke Gemini from the computer:

  • Wiggling your mouse cursor
  • Saying “Hey Google”
  • Clicking the Gemini icon in the dock
  • Clicking the Gemini icon in the Chrome taskbar

While having many entry points to Gemini makes sense, the execution feels disjointed. If you open the full Gemini app while a pop-up chat window is already open, for instance, the chat window closes and the full app cuts off your conversation, switching to a new one. The Chrome sidebar and pop-up window are also separate, so conversations in one don’t carry over to the other.

Those little inconsistencies tripped me up constantly, as I’d have to keep careful track of which conversation was happening where based on how I’d originally invoked it. Instead of just cramming AI touch points into different parts of the operating system, Google needs to do a better job of tying them all together.

There’s also a missed opportunity for Gemini to act more as an AI agent. While desktop AI apps on other platforms can work directly with files and folders on your computer, that’s currently not possible with Gemini on Googlebooks.

What’s next for Googlebooks?

Even if Googlebooks don’t feel ready now, they carry an air of inevitability. Google has already indicated that it will phase out Chrome OS by 2034, and it has outlined some vague plans for existing Chromebooks to turn into Googlebooks. Presumably that means Googlebooks will move down-market over time to include the kind of lower-end machines that defined the Chromebook business.

In the meantime, the question is whether Google will sufficiently invest in Googlebooks to address their weaknesses, instead of letting the project languish as it so often does (see: Stadia, Reader, its many attempts at social networking). One reason GoogleBooks feel so unpolished right now is because of Google’s hot-and-cold relationship with Android tablets, leading to a lack of app developer buy-in on devices with larger screens. With Google, there’s always a risk that it gets distracted by the next shiny object and leaves important work undone.

You can see how Googlebooks might eventually make sense: Combine a desktop-class Chrome experience with true Android app support, with easily available AI to help with research and automation. Maybe Google will get there someday, but first it needs to get more of the basics right.

#10626. Android gaming is having a renaissance

Good morning! Today I’m mourning the loss of Patrick Stewart by rewatching First Contact, my favorite Trek movie; beginning a marathon listen of at least one great Star Trek podcast; and replaying Elite Force and Armada, both wonderful Trek games released in 2000.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

I’m starting this edition of Inbox a bit later than I’d like, but for a good reason: I got swept up by the subject I was researching. See, I wanted to write about the seeming renaissance of gaming on Android, which has always had clear advantages and disadvantages compared to iOS. On the plus side, its openness bred experimentation and a healthy indie gaming scene, along with a thriving emulation ecosystem born of its ability to sideload apps and gain access to Android’s underlying file system. On the downside, its device and OS version fragmentation has kept some developers from attempting challenging console and PC ports, and led others to abandon their titles to bugs and time.

But thanks to a confluence of factors, as well as form factors, Android gaming is in a very good place right now. Despite Google’s continued ambivalence towards paid and premium games, the platform has received official ports of console hits like Dredge and Sifu, with others like Replaced, Absolum, and Dispatch coming soon. (One could argue things have been good for a while with Stardew Valley, Dead Cells, Balatro, Slay the Spire, and Vampire Crawlers available already, but I digress.)

Most of these games are embracing a try-before-you-buy model to avoid the upfront cost that so many mobile users resist, while others, like Dispatch, are getting a mobile optimization that reorients the experience for a portrait display.

And while traditional emulation has existed since Android was young, recent months have seen considerable improvement in breadth and performance, aided by AI coding tools and a community that wants to play its library of Steam, Windows, and Switch games on phones. This rabbit hole is extensive and varied: WinNative combines work from Winlator Bionic and Pluvia to run Windows games on Android and connect PC storefront libraries. DroidDeck aims for a SteamOS-like experience, putting Steam’s Big Picture interface on supported Android hardware with Windows games running through ARM64 Proton, which debuted recently with the Steam Frame.

It’s via DroidDeck that I whiled away a couple of glorious hours on my Galaxy Z Fold 8 playing Lumines Arise, a game perfectly suited to the pick-up-and-play nature of smartphones (though it’s best with a controller). The latest Qualcomm chips have long outpaced the mobile games they’ve been asked to power, but few knew just how well they’d run demanding PC and console titles, even through compatibility layers like Proton.

Similarly, an Android branch of the increasingly popular nxnative, which compiles Switch and Switch 2 games for iOS and macOS, has been making it easy to play games like Super Mario Bros. Wonder and Metroid Dread at 60fps on many recent Qualcomm-powered devices. There’s even a Switch 2 version in the works for Android.

The big question is whether all of this works well: will people spend more time arguing with the software than playing the games themselves? And on the legal side of the business, will publishers find success selling discounted versions of AAA titles on Android now that the translation tools are better and the device compatibility much broader?

If there’s one thing I’ve learned covering Android for nearly 20 years, it’s that the community always finds a way.

ICYMI: Ben’s Weekender essay is all about how Motorola is filling the gap OnePlus left behind, mostly.

The strangest thing I’ve seen recently is the rumor that Elon Musk wants to launch a Starlink-branded terrestrial wireless carrier in the US. Now we know how he plans to do it: by purchasing Boost Mobile from EchoStar and leveraging its contracts with AT&T and T-Mobile along with new low- and mid-band spectrum Starlink recently acquired. That infrastructure, combined with Starlink’s existing array of LEO satellites, could make for a compelling advantage over the incumbents: namely, that dead spots practically won’t exist anymore.

But as we’ve learned from countless examples over the years, running a low-margin, high-churn postpaid wireless business is not for the faint of heart, and I’m not sure why Musk has decided that now is the right time to do it.

Five years on, is the Pixel 6 series really the disaster that we remember it being? The answer, according to Damien Wilde, is a bit more nuanced.

The Pixel 6 and Pixel 6 Pro were fundamentally flawed pioneers for Google. They were the firm’s most ambitious hardware undertaking to date, and simultaneously one of the most frustrating phone series to live with during their initial launch window and beyond. If the Pixel 5 was a safe play ahead of this big pitch, the Pixel 6 was a risky dive into deep waters. It stumbled badly. Yet without those painful growing pains, the more polished, confident, and reliable Pixel devices we enjoy today simply would not exist.

Finally, networked supermarket freezers in Sweden, Belgium, and Luxembourg were hacked over the weekend, sending temperatures up to a reported 50 degrees Celsius, and all the food inside them straight into the trash.

According to Reuters, “The latest incidents follow an attack in France last month when police said hackers seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, causing fires and food losses.”

What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented. As we said earlier in the September quarter, we did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which were partly offset by the benefit of carry-in inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components. For the December quarter, we expect even higher memory costs…Looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase.

John Ternus, Apple CEO, during the company’s Q4 2026 earnings call

#10625. Employers, watch out for this trap when you lay people off

“We’re at-will. Just let them go.”

Leaders in the U.S. say these words, or something like them, with regularity. Because employment here is generally “at-will,” many assume they can terminate someone for any reason. But that misunderstands what at-will employment means—and what else is at play.

An employment decision doesn’t end when someone walks out the door. Even in at-will employment, every termination is judged in three courts: the court of law, the court of social media, and the court of public opinion. Each one can impact your business more than you realize.

The court of law

Despite what many people believe, at-will is not a magical shield against any legal liability. It doesn’t override other applicable laws, including those prohibiting discrimination, retaliation, or violations of whistleblower protections.

Most employees who leave an organization, even if they were fired, don’t sue their employer. But when they do, and if it gets to a trial, the question often isn’t whether the employer had the right to terminate them. It’s why they did.

Just ask the Society for Human Resource Management, the world’s largest HR association. In December 2025, a federal jury found SHRM liable for race discrimination and retaliation against a former employee. SHRM maintained that it followed appropriate procedures, even after the employee raised concerns of racial discrimination during her employment. But testimony and evidence at trial showed that the same individual who was responsible for investigating the employee’s complaints was also advising leaders on communications with her behind the scenes, and the employee’s termination paperwork had been drafted the same day she reported retaliation.

The jury awarded her $11.5 million. And the costs didn’t stop there.

In addition to the jury’s award and its own legal expenses, just this month, SHRM was ordered to pay more than $534,000 in attorneys’ fees for the plaintiff. Much like at-will employment, many leaders assume insurance covers everything. But SHRM’s insurer has sued to avoid paying $10 million of the verdict.

SHRM is appealing the decision. But regardless of the final outcome, it’s a reminder that employment decisions can carry significant costs in money, time, and reputation.

If it can happen to the organization that describes itself as “the global authority on work, workers, and the workplace,” it can happen to any employer.

The court of social media

Unlike a courtroom, social media doesn’t have rules of evidence or filing deadlines. There are headlines, screenshots, recordings, and sections that can shape public opinion in hours.

For many employees, a lawsuit feels intimidating and costly. Posting online does not. It feels—and is—accessible. A recorded layoff call, a screenshot of a termination email, or a “Day in the Life of Getting Fired from My Corporate Job” TikTok can reach more people in an hour than your organization reaches on LinkedIn all year.

By the time leaders start asking whether a recording is legal, it’s too late. People have made their conclusions, and continue to do so when you respond. While your lawyer may advise, “We don’t comment on personnel matters,” the public isn’t judging your legal defense. They’re evaluating whether your response reflects the values your organization claims to stand for.

After SHRM’s verdict, its CEO called it “just a blip in the history of SHRM.” That one word, “blip,” made headlines on its own.

Because in the court of social media, perception often shapes reality.

The court of public opinion

This court may have the smallest reach, but the longest memory.

One thing I learned as an employment lawyer and HR leader is that every employee is a walking billboard for your organization. People talk—to former colleagues, to friends, and to candidates, directly and on Glassdoor. And those people pay attention to what’s said, especially when a situation feels unfair.

The story spreads through their personal and professional communities. And there’s no formal appeal process in this court. Just your reputation is decided, one conversation at a time.

Use the 3-court test

None of this means that you can’t let someone go. You can, and sometimes that’s the best path, for your business and even that person. But it means that an employment decision—especially a termination—should be one that you’re comfortable defending in all three courts. Before you move forward, pause and ask:

  • Would it hold up in court? Look at the record: Did this person recently complain or take protected leave? Look at consistency: Are there others who’ve performed the same, or worse, and what happened to them? If a performance review says “Exceeds Expectations” but the termination notice says “Poor Performance,” that inconsistency won’t just concern the employee. It can raise real questions for a jury as well.
  • Would it survive a headline? Explain the decision in one sentence, as if someone who’s a complete stranger to your organization would read it. The decisions that are hardest to explain can be the ones most likely to go viral.
  • What will the team think? Not what an official statement says—what others will actually believe. Especially if the person leaving was a respected or vocal team member.

When you have doubts in any of these three areas, slow down and take a closer look.

When HR or Legal raises concerns, they’re usually not trying to create delays. They’re helping ensure the organization follows a process that is fair, defensible, and consistent.

The difference can be significant: between a fair process and Exhibit A.

A few extra days spent asking hard questions may prevent years of litigation, reputational damage, or rebuilding trust. Because at-will tells you what you’re allowed to do. It doesn’t tell you what you should do.

So, the next time someone in the room says, “We’re at-will,” ask the follow-up: “But would we win in all three courts?”

#10623. A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.

Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.

The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.

Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult

Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.

This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.

"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.

To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.

The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.

Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.

"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.

A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal

The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.

Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.

These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.

"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.

The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.

The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.

Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.

"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.

How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information

To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.

One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.

The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.

According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.

"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.

This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.

A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage

Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.

Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect."

The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.

"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.

This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.

That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.

Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor

The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.

Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.

Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.

The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.

Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.

"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small."

The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.

Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance

In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.

This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.

The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.

"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.

The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.

This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.

Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy

To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.

These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.

The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.

According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.

The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.

However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.

Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?

Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.

The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.

What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.

"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.

This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.

The research offers two potentially significant advances.

From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.

From a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.

If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.

More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.

#10621. Google’s Ocarina of Time easter egg is a blast from the past

If you’re sick of AI search and all the business of modern Google search, this week’s Google easter egg will take you back 28 years to a simpler time when Ocarina of Time was the pinnacle of gaming, and Google was still a new name.

It’s hard to believe I was sitting on a couch in my parents’ living room 28 years ago, playing Ocarina of Time on my Nintendo 64. Apparently, the folks at Google feel just as nostalgic as I do about the upcoming release of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on the Nintendo Switch 2.

Case in point, if you go to Google right now and search for “Zelda” or “Ocarina of Time,” you’ll see a Master Sword appear in the bottom-right corner of your screen. Tap that sword, and you’ll be magically transported back to the way Google looked back in 1998. It’s just seven blue links with short descriptions on a very simple page. Even the “I’m Feeling Lucky” button works!

Unfortunately, the theme only works for this specific search, so you can’t keep things looking retro if you search for anything else, even if you start from the old-school search box on the 1998-themed page. Bummer. Tapping the Master Sword again brings you back to 2026 Google search, complete with a great little animation and sounds of Link in adult or child form, depending on which way you travel in time. Try it for yourself on desktop or mobile!

#10619. The weird and brilliant innovations that led to electroconvulsive therapy—and the mystery of why it works

When I began considering electroconvulsive therapy, better known as electroshock, I assumed the “shock” part referred to the electrical zap you received. An electrode or two on your head. Some doctor pressing a button. A machine buzzed audibly. Zap, zap. You were shocked. Maybe changed forever. Maybe for good, maybe for ill. Zap, zap. Like a ray gun in a dystopian thriller. And no thriller was more dystopian (I flattered myself) than the anxious depression that had me in agony every waking moment.

Before I met those electrodes, accepted them onto my temples and into my life, my doctors gave me some books to read. I learned that most of what I thought I knew about ECT was deeply wrong. The real story was both grislier and more hopeful than you probably know. 

THE FIRST SHOCK TREATMENTS: FEVERS, INSULIN, AND ELECTROCUTED PIGS

When the Romanian-born psychiatrist Constance Pascal began using the term “shock” (choc) in her psychiatric clinic in France, around 1926, she was referring to physical treatments meant to surprise or disturb the body and brain, restoring the mind to equilibrium. Pascal considered mental illnesses to be a kind of allergic reaction, and she argued that resetting the brain and nervous system would be necessary for recovery. Pascal’s first shock therapies, in the late 1920s, used various means to prompt a reset, including induced fevers. Around the same time, in 1927 Berlin, the neurophysiologist Manfred Sakel was developing a new form of shock treatment in which a patient received potent injections of insulin. At proper doses, Sakel found he could induce a grand mal seizure as the patient came out of a hypoglycemic coma.

Insulin coma therapy produced astonishingly positive results for mood disorders—sometimes. (One famous recipient was the storied mathematician John Nash, who received insulin shocks for schizophrenia in 1961.) But results were markedly uneven. Ladislas Meduna, the Hungarian neuropathologist, shared Pascal’s interest in the possibilities of shock therapies and came to wonder whether seizures might offer a better route to healing.

In autopsies of epileptics, Meduna observed that the brains showed “tremendous changes” that were “just the opposite of those found in schizophrenia” (then a broad term that could encompass depression, schizoaffective disorders, and much more). In particular, Meduna noted that the glia—supportive cells sometimes called the janitors of the brain, whose duties include tending to our neurons—were overproduced in the brain tissue of epileptics, and vastly underrepresented in the cranial autopsies of patients with advanced mood disorders.

Pursuing this apparent antagonism between seizures and psychosis, Meduna introduced a new shock therapy in late 1934, injecting a catatonic patient with camphor, the compound then used in mothballs. Three weeks and five camphor-assisted seizures later, the patient was moving and talking—two things he hadn’t done in four years. Meduna repeated this apparent success with four subsequent patients, sometimes replacing camphor with the synthetic compound pentylenetetrazol, branded as Metrazol or Cardiazol, which achieved a similar convulsion but faster. It was also safer than insulin comas, which carried a real risk of death.

Still, Metrazol had severe drawbacks. One of the biggest was that the chemical seemed to induce feelings of absolute terror in patients before they finally fell into the coma. Not ideal for subjects already managing profound mental disturbances.

Meanwhile, in Italy, they were beginning to practice a new form of shocking the system, one that worked faster and more effectively than insulin or Metrazol—even if no one quite knew how it worked in the first place.

At the Clinic for Nervous and Mental Disorders in Rome, a little after 11 a.m. on April 11, 1938, the neurologist Ugo Cerletti placed a pair of electrodes on the temples of a man identified as “Enrico X.” Cerletti and his colleague, Lucio Bini, used a rubber band to hold the electrodes in place and electrocuted Enrico over a period of months, around 11 times. By the end of his electro-treatments, Signore X, the first ECT patient in history, was apparently recovered. The next month, in a presentation at the Royal Academy of Medicine in Rome, Cerletti and Bini administered an electro-treatment to a patient before an audience. In 1939, Cerletti and Bini coined a verb for what they’d invented: zapare, literally meaning “to zap.”

Even from the start, Cerletti was uneasy about the awesome power he commanded with those two electrodes. “When subjecting unconscious patients to such an extremely violent reaction as these convulsions, I had a sense of illicitness and felt as though I had somehow betrayed these patients,” he recalled later. Though Cerletti didn’t dwell on it, there was also the small matter of Enrico X’s relapse. He ended up readmitted to a psychiatric institution two years later.

Prehuman trials of electroconvulsions give a taste of the freewheeling sensibility that led to the development of electroshock. For example, in order to determine whether epilepsy affected the hippocampus, Cerletti as early as 1933 had sought to induce epilepsy in dogs. To do so he placed two electrodes on each dog, one inside the mouth, the other inside the rectum.

In Shock Therapy, their comprehensive 2007 history of ECT, Edward Shorter and David Healy report with dry understatement: “There was nothing innovative about this as such, and the mortality of the procedure was very high because the current passed through the dog’s heart, disrupting its electrical (pacemaker) activity.” It was an ignoble end for the dogs. For future experiments, Cerletti and Bini began placing the electrodes on a dog’s head, adequately producing a grand mal seizure.

Later, members of the Italian team visited a slaughterhouse in Rome, where dual-electrode stunning was used to render pigs unconscious before slaughter. Bini reported that after the shock, the stunned pigs reliably experienced grand mal seizures. This was precisely the seizure response that the clinicians sought in humans, and, barring extraordinarily high voltages, it carried no threat of death. (That came later, when the meat packers slit the pigs’ throats.)

ECT COMES OF AGE

Simply reading about dog rectums and pigs for slaughter, I quickly grasped the enduring stigma associated with ECT from these two details alone.

In a few of the books my doctors had recommended, I read how insulin, Metrazol, and ECT jockeyed for primacy during a period of remarkable change in neuropsychiatry, when physical treatments challenged and then overtook the formerly dominant psychoanalytic model. Then the beginning of World War II cut supply lines, making insulin prohibitively expensive or unavailable in some areas of the globe; ECT was cheaper, safer, and clinically far more attractive than either insulin or Metrazol. The war also emptied parts of Europe, notably Vienna, of many of its psychiatric eminences: Freud moved to England, Meduna went to Chicago, and the Berlin-born psychiatrist Lothar Kalinowsky, who worked on ECT in Rome under Cerletti, decamped to spread the electric gospel in London and then New York.

ECT, then, much like gin or the novel, was born in mainland Europe, refined in England, and naturalized in the States. Many American psychiatrists welcomed the practice. “Coming at a time when war is subjecting the population of the whole world to those intolerable mental strains that precipitate mental disease,” the Science News Letter wrote with excitement in 1940, “this new use of electricity for mental health instead of for death is being enthusiastically welcomed by the medical profession.”

That was the year ECT took America by storm. “In the summer of 1940, the East Coast must have literally buzzed with electricity,” Shorter and Healy write in Shock Therapy. And those who recovered often evangelized. The procedure involved some discombobulation, many patients said, perhaps some memory loss. But it had been undeniably worth it.

At least that was the case for the success stories. There were many others. The asylum era was still chugging along in the 1940s, and asylums were justly feared and hated. Among the inmates, ECT became one more blunt tool for asylum keepers to overuse, at a time when patients had precious few rights. As with fever therapy and hydrotherapy (repeated, prolonged, and often nonconsensual dousing), some asylum doctors in the 1940s and ’50s seem to have taken on ECT as a challenge: How much of this can my patients stand? Bini himself advanced an argument for the metodo dell’annichilimento, or “annihilation therapy,” which required zapping a patient multiple times a day. Other doctors picked up this method with the express purpose of rebuilding the patient’s personality from scratch.

These were tantalizing and terrifying things to read when I was deeply depressed and considering submitting to ECT myself.

THE MODERN, SOFTER SIDE OF ECT

My doctors told me that today’s ECT was quite different. No one was doing annihilation therapy in the U.S. anymore, one said. Plus, modern or “modified” ECT was much more civilized because the electrical pulses were briefer and more targeted, and the doctors gave you anesthesia and muscle relaxers and even an oxygen tube to prevent asphyxia. All the horror stories, my psychiatrist said, dated from the era of “unmodified” ECT. “We’re past the grisly stuff now,” he told me.

But that didn’t make the history any easier to read.

Yes, anesthesia and tranquilizers entered the picture—particularly in 1951, with the introduction of the muscle relaxant succinylcholine, still used in ECT today. But many asylums and hospitals were slow to adopt these new, gentler practices. According to the science journalist and ECT skeptic Robert Whitaker, more than 1 million patients got forced ECT in the 1940s and ’50s. Even kids didn’t escape the electrodes. From 1942 to 1947, Bellevue Hospital in New York treated 98 children, some as young as 4, with a long sequence of ECT treatments.

My heart rate slowed a bit when I read about the softer side of ECT. It’s considered sufficiently gentle to be offered as a first resort for elderly patients who can’t tolerate SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) or other pharmacological interventions. I was even more surprised to learn that ECT didn’t attain its stigma—its association with persecution and alleged brain damage—until the mid-1960s, thanks in part to emerging psychopharmaceuticals but mainly amid a frantic new campaign to abolish ECT.

THE CAMPAIGN AGAINST ECT

The antipsychiatry movement was a coalition between heterodox psychiatrists and members of the New Left. It emerged at a time when the antiauthoritarian ethos of young baby boomers came into conflict with a procedure that recalled the tyranny of asylum medicine. “Shock resonated because, like nuclear energy, [ECT] had the aura of an out-of-control technology imposed by an authoritarian society,” observed the journalist Larry Tye, who, with Kitty Dukakis, authored an illuminating 2006 book about electroshock. By the 1970s, Tye reported, detractors had begun “picket[ing] outside electroshock clinics with signs linking the practitioners to Spanish inquisitor Tomás de Torquemada and Nazi executioner Adolf Eichmann.” The anti-ECT campaign has been vigorous and well funded, thanks not least to munificent contributions from the Church of Scientology, which has also played a central role in organizing.

Accordingly, ECT therapy was severely curtailed in most parts of the country. Numbers are tricky, as there’s no central trove of data, but the most plausible estimate is that the yearly number of ECT patients in the U.S. fell from around 300,000 in the 1950s and ’60s to around 59,000 by 1975; by 1980, that number had dropped further, to around 32,000. “It is as though penicillin had suddenly gone into a decline in the absence of any objective circumstance that might discourage physicians from prescribing it or patients from accepting it,” Shorter and Healy wrote.

One can understand the skepticism. I know I did. But as I read about the campaign to expunge ECT, I wondered whether the problem was a failure to distinguish the baby from the bathwater. It seems statistically undeniable that, during ECT’s period in the wilderness, millions of depressed or bipolar or schizophrenic Americans were functionally denied recourse to ECT. One doctor told me we’d never know how many died because ECT was drummed out of so many American hospitals. ECT’s frequently lurid portrayals in popular culture only bolstered the eye-popping claims of the antipsychiatry camp: ECT turns you into a zombie; it erases your entire memory; it will literally break your back.

I found a few books that mounted a defense of ECT. Sometimes half-apologetic, other times closer to triumphant. I read the Shorter and Healy history, Carrie Fisher’s memoir about electroshock, and Tye’s book with Dukakis, entitled Shock: The Healing Power of Electroconvulsive Therapy. (“In some ways ECT is less traumatic for me than going to the dentist, and certainly less frightening than the root canal,” Dukakis wrote.)

But when I tried to find some authoritative consensus about memory loss, I kept meeting a chorus of contradiction from the medical literature. Some doctors said memory loss would be mild; others said it could be “more pronounced” (than what?); but the third and loudest group said that memory loss was a canard, a talking point for antipsychiatrists, adding that most patients reported few to no cognitive problems. When I went online to eavesdrop on patient forums, the consensus was clearer: Memory loss is very, very real.

I’m only speculating here, but I do wonder whether, in their zeal to defend a lifesaving treatment from demagogic skeptics, some ECT advocates may have pushed back with their own immoderate claims. Whatever the cause, it’s a strange experience to have different doctors tell you different things about what’s about to happen to your memory. It’s even stranger when, after a few treatments, you can’t quite remember which doctor told you what.

GENERATING NEW NEURONS (AND OFTEN HOPE)

The most baffling, endlessly intriguing questions about ECT are how and why it works. Physicians since ancient times have recorded the sometimes salutary effects of seizures on certain forms of mental illness, yet even today we don’t know precisely why a given brain is happier, or clearer, or calmer, following a few seizures. There’s an old saw comparing ECT to aspirin: We don’t know how it works, but it works magnificently. Still, a few general ideas about the mechanism of ECT are widely accepted.

During the seizure, affected neurons all fire at the same time, several times per second. Some doctors refer to this effect as the brain “resetting” itself. As a result of this firing, the brain releases a welcome surplus of neurohormones such as norepinephrine and neurotransmitters such as dopamine. The most intriguing recent account for ECT’s high rate of response—often reported at around 75% to 80% for major depressives who’ve failed to find relief with pharmacology—is that the release of these brain chemicals can stimulate neural growth across various regions of the brain. Per brain imaging, just a few ECT treatments are often enough to spur visible volume increases in multiple cortical regions, not least in the hippocampus, the area of the brain that is prey to atrophy during major depression and other maladies, including addiction, certain schizoaffective disorders, dementia, and Alzheimer’s.

ECT’s demonstrated neurogenetic properties offer a compelling explanation for why the treatment remains a most effective antidepressant. That the brain grows and shows markedly more, and more regular, activity after ECT treatment is potentially confusing to lay­ people, many of whom take the treatment to be inherently damaging—­“scarring” is the preferred participle among the skeptics, as though doctors have applied a knife or a white-hot poker to your brain. Of course, surprisingly little electricity goes through you; not enough to singe or scar. Comparisons are tricky, because the human machine and, say, the refrigerator require different currents, but the amount of energy that zaps you during a single ECT session is mercifully modest—perhaps the equivalent of charging your phone by 1% or powering a lightbulb for a few seconds.

Discoveries about hippocampal growth after ECT are straightforwardly exciting. For those of us who grew up in the 1980s and ’90s, the essential unrecuperability of brain cells and memories was treated as a basic fact in “just say no”–style antidrug campaigns and even biology class. That was all wrong, even then. Neurogenesis had been established in small mammals and birds by the 1980s, while in the 1990s, we discovered that the human brain has its own stem cells—pluripotent little guys that can become new neurons, sometimes creating new connections that support neuroplasticity, as well as fresh glial cells to clean and maintain the brain’s circuits.

Still, certain disagreements persist. Some of the keenest students and proponents of ECT believe the seizure is the crucial mechanism, while other experts argue it’s the body’s postseizure response that hits the reset button, rather than the seizure itself. If the latter group is right, that opens the intriguing possibility that future advances in brain imaging and brain stimulation might reveal a gentler shortcut toward triggering an anticonvulsive response, hypergenerating these chemicals, and reinvigorating the hippocampus and its neighbors, all without the dreaded seizure.

Regardless, ECT remains the nuclear power of psychiatric treatment: much maligned, often misused, yet sturdy and powerful, the gold standard that we’ve somehow disowned. Among latter-day electrical treatments, which include transcranial magnetic stimulation and vagus nerve stimulation, none thus far has shown the efficacy of modern ECT. Particularly for acute cases—people who might not have the time to wait for another drug to work or not to work—ECT is unmatched.

It could also be on the verge of becoming much more effective. Cutting-edge research into ultrabrief pulses and hypertargeted forms of the treatment offer the tantalizing possibility that future patients might receive greater benefits with fewer side effects. But we’re not there yet.

There are, of course, legitimate lines of skepticism. Some skeptics raise reasonable methodological points. For example, while we can draw on various controlled trials into ECT’s efficacy, placebo-controlled trials—in which a control group undergoes a sham version of the treatment—are rare, largely because they raise major ethical concerns. (Fooling a depressive into thinking he’s had a seizure is both tricky and mean.)

The other major concerns involve consent and side effects. In the U.K., for example, there are complaints that some older patients, especially women, have received ECT against their will, and that doctors have minimized side effects, leaving patients shaken when they discover unexpected memory deficits.

Today, the anti-ECT movement is gaining ground again. In the U.S., opponents have once again taken to the courts, where litigation over undisclosed risks helped push one manufacturer of ECT machines into bankruptcy in 2021. A separate lawsuit produced a 2026 settlement from two psychiatrists accused of understating potential harms.

As a journalist rather than a researcher, all I can say with certainty is what I’ve seen empirically in myself and other patients: ECT can have miraculous-seeming positive effects for the deeply depressed. It also verifiably inhibits the consolidation of more recent memories. My treatment was voluntary, and I lost access to more of the previous months than I’d been prepared for. What I got in exchange, though, was real healing; slow at first, then undeniable. Without ECT, I could’ve harmed myself and continued courting death. Instead, I returned to life in all its mess and splendor. Historically, ECT has indeed been much abused. But among the many ways to abuse ECT is withholding it from a patient whose life it could save.

Excerpted from Jolt: My Electric Journey Out of Darkness by Ted Scheinman. Published by Simon & Schuster. Copyright © 2026 by Ted Scheinman. All rights reserved.
