#10618. Redmagic 12 Pro review: You’ve never gamed on a phone like this before

The Redmagic 12 Pro impresses with a Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor, liquid cooling, a fan, plus a massive 8,400mAh battery to keep the games going for hours and hours.

As I sat in my living room with my family, playing Monster Hunter Outlanders together on the Redmagic 12 Pro, I completely forgot I was playing on a phone. The game looked perfect. It ran at a locked 60FPS and hadn’t dropped frames since I began playing over an hour ago. It just felt like I was back in college, playing Monster Hunter Freedom on my PSP with my friends in the same room.

Most other phones at this point would have throttled hard. What began at 60FPS almost certainly would have been 40FPS tops after 30 minutes or so; the frame drops during heavy fights would have been even worse, but the Redmagic 12 Pro didn’t skip a beat. Even after a solid hour of playing, the battery had only dropped 10%, completely erasing all concerns about using my phone as a gaming console.

This thing is the real deal, and while I’ve used plenty of high-performance phones and gaming phones over the years, none have quite nailed it as this one has. Now, with my Redmagic 12 Pro and my trusty GameSir G8 Galileo, I can game whenever and wherever I want without battery anxiety or thermal problems. Redmagic has gotten really good at this gaming thing.

Sustained gaming performance is difficult to pull off on a phone, which is why the Redmagic 12 Pro features two types of active cooling: a fan and liquid cooling. This design builds on last year’s with a larger liquid cooling system and a more efficient fan. The intake and exhaust vents are on the sides of the phone, not the back, ensuring these shouldn’t get easily blocked. Despite this, the phone is IP68 and IP69 rated.

Most modern phones have huge camera islands that make them awkward to use in controllers, but the Redmagic 12 Pro features a completely flat build that fits perfectly in *any* controller. I don’t usually like overly flat builds, but it actually suits this phone’s purpose.

This should mean the phone does exceedingly well in benchmarks, but I have the distinct feeling the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 processor inside is making that overly difficult. I don’t have any other SD8 Elite Gen 6 phones just yet, but rumor has it that this is one *hot* chipset. I saw the phone hit 50C during testing, so that definitely seems to be the case.

In 3DMark Solar Bay Extreme, a benchmark that stresses ray-tracing performance over 20 minutes, the Redmagic 12 Pro started at 2065 points and ended at 1169 on its last run. That’s a 43% drop in performance over a 20-minute period, which is in line with passively-cooled phones like the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Regardless, the initial performance is nearly double the S26 Ultra, while the 1169 end score matches the S26 Ultra’s best score and is roughly 35% higher than the S26 Ultra’s sustained performance score of around 860.

Actual gaming seemed to fare better in my testing, where I saw sustained performance consistently outperform any Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 phone I have in my possession. When running Wanderstop through the phone’s built-in Steam emulation (more on that soon), the Redmagic 12 Pro averaged 72FPS at the highest settings. Other phones with SD8 Elite Gen 5 processors scored half that, at best. Native Android games like Monster Hunter Outlanders worked even better.

But it’s not just performance that sets this phone apart; it’s the gaming features. Redmagic has fully leaned into the mobile gaming power user angle with its software. Pressing and holding the red button on the right side of the phone launches Gravity X, the built-in game launcher that keeps all your games in one place. It even features an embedded Steam emulator, so all you need to do is sign in with your Steam account and download anything in your library.

Overall performance on Steam games is impressive, but like any emulation, not everything is going to work. Hogwarts Legacy worked near-flawlessly at medium settings, but titles like Star Wars Galactic Racer wouldn’t run at all. Other apps that run Steam games, like DroidDeck and Game Native, also work, but the Adreno 850 GPU doesn’t have official support on those apps yet, so compatibility is very hit or miss (mostly miss) for now.

The Redmagic 12 Pro’s in-game menu is also unlike anything you’ve ever seen. It’s not just jam-packed with information, but has a boatload of bespoke features. One custom mapping tool lets you map the triggers (yes, this phone has capacitive triggers on the side) to any on-screen virtual key.

Another utility records all the time, Xbox/PS5/Switch style, and saves a clip at the touch of a floating button. Yet another features on on-screen AI anime character that can interact with your games and even give you gameplay feedback. You can even enable frame gen and Super Resolution in any game. It’s wild.

All this is wrapped up in an incredibly impressive hardware package, with loud, clear speakers, an excellent 185Hz AMOLED display (that uses DC dimming and 2160Hz PWM for eye comfort), with 5,000-nit peak brightness. I measured the actual HDR brightness at 2300-nits, so this can get nice and bright when it needs to.

If there was ever a phone that could play games and still get you through a full day’s normal phone usage, it’s this one. Passthrough charging is also supported, too, so you can keep the battery from getting overcharged or overheated while gaming for hours.

As is the case with many laser-focused devices like this, the camera is the low point of the experience. It’s got a 50MP rear camera and a 50MP ultra wide. Both get the job done, but they’ll never impress you.

The 16MP 9th-generation under display camera looks impressive on the surface — you can’t see it at all, even with light shining off the display — but the results are still far from good. Redmagic uses an AI algorithm to substantially enhance the overall quality, which cleans up the image nicely but exhibits lots of hallucinations. Just look at my eyes in the above picture. It’s not good.

Thankfully, the Android 17-based Redmagic OS 12 software is quite good. Visually, it reminds me of a mix of AOSP and Samsung’s One UI. Lots of expected features are here — an AI wallpaper generator, call screening, recording with transcripts, writing help, etc — plus all the awesome gaming-focused tools and quite a bit of customization across the OS.

It’s a great overall experience, but Redmagic only offers software updates for 3 years, so this one won’t stay around as long as some other phones. If you’re more interested in mobile gaming than anything — especially if you want a phone that can easily run Steam games in addition to mobile stuff — this is an impressively good choice.

#10616. Adobe’s SVP of design believes it’s a golden age of design. Hear him out

It’s never been easier to make an image. Even for people who don’t consider themselves creative, translating an idea into an illustration, graphic, video—any format, really—is now as simple as typing a prompt into a box (quality not guaranteed). 

Adobe knows this. The company, which has long been the tool of choice for professional creatives, is now looking to “aggressively acquire the next generation of Adobe loyalists,” as the outgoing CEO, Shantanu Narayen, put it during a recent earnings call. That means bringing the not-so-creative among us into the fold with tools like Firefly AI and Adobe Express. Even its professional-grade tools are eyeing novice creatives with AI agents that make navigating complex tools easier.

The strategy appears to be working. So far this year, Adobe has increased the number of “Creative freemium” users—people using free versions of Firefly and Adobe Express—by 70%, reaching 100 million monthly active users. Meanwhile, its professional-focused business remains healthy and growing, though at a slower rate (15% year over year as of Q3).

As Adobe kicks off its biggest event of the year with its Adobe Max conference, Fast Company spoke with Eric Snowden, Adobe’s SVP of design, about what this push into freemium means for the way his team thinks about designing tools, the challenges of bringing Adobe products into third-party apps like ChatGPT, and why this might truly be the most exciting time to be a designer. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Fast Company: For the last few years, Adobe has really pushed its identity as a company that makes creative tools for everyone—not just professional designers, but also people who don’t necessarily consider themselves designers at all. I’d love to understand what the business imperative for that broader definition of a creator is to you and Adobe more broadly.

Eric Snowden: I think this has been a trend for Adobe for longer than the last few years. I mean, if you go back and look at things like Elements and other products, we’ve been trying to bring creativity to more and more people for many years. And I think between technology that’s come up—mobile and now AI—we can just go broader and broader than we’ve ever been able to do before. Adobe’s really been about empowering people to express themselves and to communicate in new ways. And that’s been at the core of our company’s mission for a long time. We’re just able to do that in ways we haven’t been able to do before.

I think it’s been accelerated, but I don’t know that it’s a completely new thing for us. And I think you’re seeing more and more people want to do this, right? I think whether it’s through social media or other forums, people want to express themselves in new ways, and they’ve got new forums to do that. And so, as demand has grown, I think we’ve really wanted to meet that demand for a broader audience.

Back in June, your outgoing CEO said, “We believe now is the time to aggressively acquire the next generation of Adobe loyalists.” And to just kind of push that idea a little bit more, why is that so important?

We have an easier on-ramp now than we’ve ever had before. I think whether it’s products like Express that anyone can pick up and use, or it’s the new technology, like agents or other things we brought into our flagship tools, . . . it’s just easier to be creative than it’s ever been.

I started using Adobe products when I was a teenager. I’ve always been a big believer that people pick their first creative tools when they’re really young, and we have a lot of data around that. . . . Maybe they become a creative, and maybe they don’t. But it’s something that people start pretty young, and so we want to make sure that we’ve got a really great on-ramp for folks who want to be creative.

For me, it was creating posters and websites for the band I was in, and I didn’t know that was going to lead me into being the SVP of design at Adobe. I didn’t even know design was a career at that point, but I think that on-ramp exposed me to this entire world that I didn’t know existed.

Obviously the on-ramp that you experienced is very different from the on-ramp a 14-year-old might experience today. How would you characterize that difference? How are you trying to reach that younger generation of potential creative?

There are so many different ways. One is, where they can express themselves is extremely different. I didn’t have social networks or other places to express myself. I think that’s a big part of it. At the time, we only had high-end professional specialist tools, and so I was using Photoshop to make a poster for a band that felt a little bit like taking a 747 to go to the grocery store. It was just overkill for what I needed. I think today I might have used something like Adobe Express to do that, but that could have introduced me in a much easier way and an on-ramp to the things I need today. 

But I also love the approach we’re taking with agents inside of our professional tools, because it feels like a guide that can bring you into something like Photoshop or even After Effects. I was playing with the After Effects agent a week or so ago, and the beauty of it is you can prompt your way into the product, but under the hood, it is still After Effects. I liken it to a self-driving car where it’s doing its thing, but at any moment you can drive the wheel and you have full control. It’s got all of the layers and all the keyframes and the easings and everything underneath it, so at any moment where you want to get in and tweak every knob and dial, that’s there for you. 

Most of us at Adobe, we think a lot about how we learned Adobe’s products and how we can make that easier. That’s something that has stuck in my head for the entirety of my time at Adobe. And I think a lot about how we make it easier for someone to learn these tools than it was for me, because the ceiling is so high in these tools, which is the beauty of them. But we want to make that first step or two into them as seamless and as low as possible.

So what does that look like? Can you give me a good example of how you’ve made the accessibility clear?

Yeah, one of the things I just mentioned, right? Bringing agents into our tools, I think, is one way. Another way is, there are brand new tools that are easier to pick up that are specialized. So, something like using Adobe Fresco on the iPad for drawing. It’s on a specialized device that is great for working in that way. It’s a tool that is dedicated for that use case. There are also things in our flagship tools. Like one example I always give is the properties panel in Illustrator, and this is getting a little nerdy, but we took all of these different panels and combined them into a single panel, right? We didn’t take away anything. All those other panels already exist, but we gave people a single place to access most of the things they need, and that just simplifies getting to know a product when you come in for the first time. But it actually doesn’t take anything away from our power users.

One of the the fun, but also really hard, tensions of this job is: How do you change things in our existing tools to make it easier for new people to onboard without disrupting the fact that professionals have very specific, bespoke workflows that if you change a a pixel or two, you can really throw them off of their game. It’s like it’s a musical instrument to them. You can’t move the keys on a keyboard—it’s the same thing, and so I think it’s about finding that balance. And so it’s something we’re thinking about all the time, like across the portfolio.

I would love to understand how your team designs a single product for someone who has never opened Photoshop, let’s say, and for someone who’s used it for like 20 years, right? Are those two different products in your mind? Two different experiences?

I’m glad you brought that up as an example because we recently launched this AI-assisted mode in Photoshop, and I think the goal with that is to have a dedicated place that people can land who have never used Photoshop before. It’s very simplified; an AI-centric experience, like a workspace where they can go in and they can prompt their way to editing their image, but they are still in the context of Photoshop. It is one click away to get the more full-featured interface, and there’s sort of this interplay between the two where they can graduate from this simple interface into the full interface. 

Now they don’t have to do that, right? They could have a full editing experience in this simplified interface, and people can go from the more complex interface into the simplified one if they wanted to. But I think it’s about bringing them into the entire tool, giving them an experience that you know. Again, it’s about that first step or two. It’s like: What is that day one experience like, and giving them something they feel like they can digest and they get a result that they’re proud of as quickly as possible. 

I was a Photoshop teacher at Parsons [School of Design] for a number of years, and when I was teaching Photoshop, it was really about how do I spend the least amount of time possible to get someone to have an image that comes out the other end that they feel proud of. Because once they did that, they were willing to invest the time to learn the breadth and depth of one of the most powerful pieces of software on the planet. You can do anything in Photoshop. That’s the beauty of it. And so it’s about how do we give them that success as quickly as possible, and then we sort of guide them through the rest of it and show them the depth of this kind of amazing tool.

Earlier this year Jesus Diaz wrote about how Adobe is rolling out a new integration for ChatGPT, which effectively lets users, @ Adobe in ChatGPT’s interface, and then use natural language to accomplish whatever it is they want to accomplish, pulling from the capabilities from across Creative Cloud apps. 

What was interesting to me about that announcement was that it was sort of an acknowledgement that many of the people who are new to Adobe products are not going to use them in the same way, or onboard in the same way, that you all are accustomed to. As someone who is designing these products, I’m curious what challenges it creates for you and your team when somebody has access to Creative Cloud through third-party apps like Claude or ChatGPT or Gemini?

We think a lot about continuity across experiences because, to your point, there will be some people that are introduced to it through ChatGPT, and then do experience it through our flagship applications. We want to make sure they have an experience that doesn’t feel like they have to start over when they come into our products. We talk a lot about skills transfers—this idea that if they build a skill in one place and they go to a second place, that skill is something that was a good investment for them that they can build on top of. We want to make sure that the pieces of the interface that we bring into these third parties, as they learn those, those things are valuable to them as they progress. 

We also realize there will be some people that will stay in ChatGPT. There will be some people that go the other direction—people who are using our flagship tools and then find it in ChatGPT want to make sure the skills transfer goes the other way. And so that continuity of experience is one part of it. But I think the most important thing, and the thing that is unique about Adobe’s approach to all of this, is we’re a workflow company. People aren’t usually coming to us to use a single feature, a single product. They are trying to accomplish a goal, and they are often using a product or a couple of products to accomplish something much larger.

And so we need to make sure that all of this stuff works together, whether it’s a couple of Adobe tools or an Adobe tool and a third-party tool. Because as a workflow company, that’s what people expect from us and often come to us for. That can be a challenge when you don’t control the full end to end, but that’s something we’re really trying to make sure we get right for our customers.

Talking about the freemium model, your freemium monthly active users have increased a lot over the past year. How does that change the way that you think about designing Adobe’s products? And how are you thinking about graduating them into a paid tier? 

Yeah, it’s interesting. I think it goes back to the previous challenge of new users, and they’re tied together, even though freemium doesn’t always equate to new. But it is about giving people value and feeling an accomplishment as soon as possible. And in a freemium model, you’re allowed to give them that without having to have a sign-in or a paywall be the first thing that someone experiences.  

When people think of Photoshop, they do think of this sort of unlimited potential, but they still don’t even know what is possible with Photoshop. And so, the more we can show them what these tools are capable of, the more we can get them excited. And I think in these new models, we’re allowed to show them more of that before we ask them to sign up or to pay for something. That is beneficial to Adobe, right? We can show them like the magic that we can give to them; that’s really exciting to be able to show versus tell, and I think the freemium model allows us to do more of that. 

It’s a real value exchange with a customer. At some point, we’re saying, ‘give us either your email or your money,’ and it’s clear what value we’re exchanging with them. And I think doing that at the right time, that’s when conversion happens. If you’re doing that at the wrong time, I think that makes conversion more difficult. That is a design challenge to figure out, when does that handshake happen? I think you get the best conversion numbers where there’s the right there’s the right balance. If you have it too far on one side, the user feels like they haven’t gotten enough to warrant whatever you’re asking them to do. And if it’s too far on the other side, that’s not good for the business. And so I think it’s about finding that right balance where everyone benefits from that exchange.

It’s an interesting time to be talking about this with the Canva news [last] week, with the company laying off or restructuring around 22% of its workforce. Part of those pressures, it seems, comes from the pressures of building a product that caters to a very large base of people who use the tool for free, but are also using very compute-intensive features. Obviously, Adobe has a different business model. You’re a completely different company—this is not apples to apples. But I’m curious because we’re here: What did that news reveal to you? 

Yeah, it’s. I mean, it’s an interesting question. I mean, obviously we saw that news, but you know, I frankly try not to think about that too much. Canva’s doing interesting things out there, but I think we have to keep focused on what we’re doing, and I think we are doing something very different. I think we are a very different company. I mean, to your point, creativity is a piece of our business, but we have other massive lines of business that are connected to creativity. But they do one thing, and we do a multitude of things, and we do a multitude of things that are all interconnected. And so, it’s just kind of hard to make that comparison in a lot of ways.

One thing that I wanted to talk about is a data point that you all came up with in a survey from back in the summer about small business owners and creative marketing. It says the average small business owner fills five roles a day, adding up to 200 extra hours a year; 44% act as their own marketer; 41% act as social media manager, and 35% as creative director. 

Those are pretty crazy numbers. It makes total sense to me that that’s the case, but just seeing the numbers kind of blows my mind. When did you all suspect this shift was happening,? Is this an AI-enabled change in the way that people run their businesses?

This shift has been happening for a while, but I think it’s been nearly impossible for people to keep up with this. Just the burden that’s put on these businesses, it’s pretty wild, and I think AI could be part of the solution to that.

But the demands and expectations on small businesses are also echoed in enterprises and everything else. Like the demand for content is at an all-time high, and it is growing. There’s just insane expectations for all these different channels . . . it just keeps scaling, keeps getting bigger and bigger. And I think that’s where the opportunity for us is to help, whether it’s tools like Express, where people can do some of this stuff themselves if they need to; whether it’s through agents; whether it’s through empowering professionals to do this work faster and better.

Our industry focuses a lot about productivity with AI, but we don’t talk enough about the fact that there are things that we can do now that we could not do before. Yes, all of us are being asked to do more, and yes, everybody’s being asked to work faster. But my team talks a lot about, what can we do now that we couldn’t do six months ago? The fact that we can build our own tools and our own plugins, or the fact that people who couldn’t do motion graphics can add that to their toolkit. I mean I think it’s really about not just the productivity part of AI, but raising the ceiling on either the breadth of work people can do, or the quality of work people can do. I think it’s about finding the balance between those two things in a lot of ways.

Your team can do things that it wasn’t able to do six months ago. Any thoughts on what you’d like to be able to do in six months that you can’t do now?

When it comes to my team in particular, I know there’s a lot of concern in the design community about what it means to be a product designer. I think that’s fair because the world is changing, and we all have to acknowledge that. But when I talk to my team, I think this is actually one of the most exciting times to be a product designer. In the past, if you were a designer and you had an idea that you were passionate about, you would have to convince someone to build that idea. Either find an engineering friend or a partner who was up for it, and convince them to help build a prototype with you, or convince a product manager who controlled engineering resources that this was a good idea. 

You don’t really need to do that anymore. You can just build it yourself. I know people are founding companies where it’s a bunch of designers and a single engineer, and I think the power that designers have to go just do things on their own is unprecedented, and I mean that literally. I think as time goes on, that is going to just get greater. And so, if you project six months into the future, what people can build is going to be amazing.

I would say a good portion of the software that I run on my computer these days, whether it’s Photoshop plug-ins I built, or software that I’m using to to make myself more productive, I’ve written myself; bespoke things for me that is running alongside Adobe software that I use or connected to it to make myself more productive. That’s a really interesting world that we’re entering into, and I can see that accelerating. For product designers who really embrace that, that is an exciting new world, but it is a very different world than the one we’re living in today, or certainly one we’ve lived in historically. I think if people lean into that, there’s something really fascinating and interesting there—and fun.

I think we should occasionally talk about the fact that as a designer, being able to just build stuff is really fun. It reminds me of the Flash days of the internet where anything felt possible, and I haven’t felt that way in a long time.

#10615. Three Ds for a successful AI rollout

Do you remember Juicero? It was a $400 Wi-Fi-connected juicer that only worked with proprietary fruit packets, each costing as much as a juice from the store. After a much-hyped launch, the company tanked magnificently when it was discovered that the packets could simply be squeezed by hand, making the machine virtually useless.

Juicero was a classic case of a product built to solve a problem that didn’t exist. It was a shiny, expensive gadget that offered no real value. Swap “gadget” for “platform” and you have an apt description of what happens all too often with AI today. Fortunately, most companies have the internal resources to sidestep that pitfall, using what I call the “three Ds”: discuss, deputize, and dismiss.

DISCUSS

Too often, AI decisions are made behind closed doors among the higher-ups. By the time employees are brought in, the question isn’t whether AI makes sense for the organization, but which targets they need to hit with it: “Every employee must add XYZ agents to their workflow by Q3,” for example.

The result is graveyards of unmaintained agents, teams burning budget on lackluster AI applications to satisfy their bosses (tokenmaxxing, anyone?), and employees who feel AI is being done to them rather than for them. To borrow from Juicero: Ask employees whether they need the expensive appliance, or whether they can just as easily squeeze the juice by hand.

Employees will become the first line of defense against costly AI deployments when the directive to use AI comes from leadership. Managers should ask their teams where AI could make a difference in their workloads, what other tasks they could tackle if AI removed some of their to-dos, and what controls they’d need to make that work. Only when a fuller picture comes into view should the C-suite commit to major AI investments.

DEPUTIZE

The people best positioned to make AI adoption stick are those who’ve always sought out automation to free up time for focused work. Good leadership deputizes them.

At Moments Lab, our technical champion is Olivier, who runs our infrastructure. He was automating things long before agents existed: Slack routines so he’d get pinged less, self-service tools for access requests, and anything else where he spotted a repeating pattern of questions and asked himself how to make it go away. You don’t recruit that kind of person, you notice them.

Giving champions room means giving them resources and proximity to decision-making. Carve out a meaningful slice of their time, say 20%, to experiment. Include them in leadership conversations so they can shape strategy based on what they’ve learned. Ideally, pair someone with deep technical chops, like Olivier, with someone client-facing and human-centric. Between them, they’ll catch the problems worth solving and the solutions people will use.

Finally, make their work visible. Open an internal channel where champions share what worked, what failed, and what surprised them. Colleagues who see a tedious process eliminated or an hour reclaimed will want in. Leadership sets the direction; champions make it contagious.

DISMISS

Named by economist Richard Thaler and first studied by psychologists Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer, the sunk-cost fallacy is the tendency to keep investing in something that’s failing because of how much you’ve already put into it.

With AI, it tends to take the form of zombie deployments: the pilot that’s been “three months from proving itself” for a year and a half, the enterprise license renewed because canceling would mean admitting a mistake, or the fleet of agents no one maintains. The spend becomes its own justification.

Other failures are harder to spot because they look like success. We built an autonomous agent to post a Monday recap in Slack. Its first source of truth was our company values, and since our first value is optimism, it started reframing lost deals as good news, until the sales team objected. The same agent later wrote a thank-you message to a departing colleague, drawing on their work across Slack and Notion, before any human had said a word. The message was warm and accurate, but letting a machine say goodbye first sent the wrong signal from leadership.

Elsewhere, agents raised our pull request volume so much that our most senior engineers became full-time reviewers and stopped building. And an AI-generated summary that is sent without being read by a human first simply pushes the work onto the recipient. At scale, the daily volume of text to reread becomes a management problem in its own right.

The way out is to decide what failure looks like before you deploy anything. Set clear success metrics up front, put a review cadence on the calendar, and give someone explicit authority to pull the plug. Killing an underperforming tool isn’t a defeat; it’s clearing the counter for something that works. Nobody’s obligated to keep buying Juicero packets just because they paid $400 for the machine.

AI PROJECTS GATHERING DUST

Gartner estimated earlier this year that around 50% of generative AI projects end in failure, shelved next to the Juicero and countless other solutions started in earnest but without proper planning. Sticking to the three Ds lowers the odds of choosing the wrong path and then throwing good money after bad. So grab your team a round of (real) smoothies, have those conversations first, and then start building.

Phil Petitpont is cofounder and CEO of Moments Lab.

#10613. Google has fixed Android Auto issues on Samsung Galaxy phones running One UI 9 [U]

Samsung’s Android 17-based One UI 9 update is rolling out more widely and, with it, some apparent issues with Android Auto on some Galaxy phones.

Update 11/3: Speaking to 9to5Google, Google has confirmed that “a fix has been rolled out” for Android Auto issues on Galaxy devices running One UI 9.

In the time since Samsung’s stable Android 17 update started rolling out, there have been reports popping up around Android Auto issues. Reports of these problems have shown up on Reddit, Samsung’s forums, and Google’s forums.

It’s not a massively widespread problem as far as we can tell, but there’s a clear pattern and enough reports to suggest a trend. Those affected report issues with stuttering performance and/or the connection failing entirely.

The folks at Android Authority found one user test where a Galaxy S25 Edge on One UI 8.5 lacked any issues, but a Galaxy S24 Ultra running One UI 9 immediately reproduced the issues that other users have been reporting. It’s hardly a scientific test, but it shows that One UI 9 is probably responsible for some of this odd behavior.

There’s been no official word on a fix just yet. Let us know in the comments below if you’re dealing with any issues.

#10612. OpenAI wants to be Google

OpenAI wants to be Google. The company would likely reject the idea publicly, but think about the economics of advertising. Google built one of the best businesses in history by putting companies in front of people at the moment they say they need something. People forget how big that business is.

Google generated nearly $295 billion in advertising revenue last year. Search and other properties alone produced $225 billion—about $4.3 billion a week. The Trade Desk, the largest independent demand-side platform, booked $2.9 billion in annual revenue. Google’s search business generates more revenue in an average week than The Trade Desk does in a year. ChatGPT now sits at the same moment of expressed intent that Google has monetized so effectively. Whatever OpenAI calls its ad business, that is the prize.

CHATGPT SHOWS INTENT

Consider how you use tech products. You open Instagram to lean back and scroll. You don’t need anything, but maybe something catches your eye. You open Google because you need a new blue sweater. That’s high intent.

Specific searching is the way in which many people use ChatGPT. This is the important part. Nobody types “sweater” into ChatGPT. They say they need something warm for a week in Chicago in January. They add that wool makes them itch and that they’d rather not spend more than $150. Those prompts become a brief. We hand over our wishes, must-haves, constraints, and worries. Then we compare options and decide.

That comparison is where every sweater brand wants to be standing, and OpenAI has started selling the spot. Advertisers can buy on a CPM or CPC basis through OpenAI’s beta self-service Ads Manager, measure conversions with a pixel and Conversions API, and access campaign-level performance reporting. OpenAI is also testing Sponsored Agents, which let a user start a separate conversation with an advertiser after clicking an ad.

So the plumbing exists.

A SEARCH-CALIBER AD PLATFORM

But what made Google an unrivalled profit machine is that the advertiser can see the demand. I pick the keywords I want. I get a report of the searches that triggered my ads. I see which searches turned into customers and which burned money, and I block the losers with negative keywords. ChatGPT gives me nothing comparable yet. My ad shows up next to a conversation, and I have no idea what kind of conversation it was.

OpenAI needs to build analytics that show advertisers the consumer intent based on their prompts. I want to know which categories of intent my impressions ran against. I want to know whether those people were exploring, comparing, or ready to act, and which needs and product criteria drove that engagement. I want to know which kinds of sweater prompts turned into business and, just as important, which didn’t. Google’s advertisers have had some version of that map for two decades. It’s why brands keep paying.

Of course, privacy is always a concern. People might be telling ChatGPT things they would never type into a search box, and no advertiser should get to read a conversation or see an individual prompt. Fine. Nobody is asking for that, and it isn’t an excuse. Google has worked around the same problem for decades. It limits, aggregates, and buckets the queries too rare to show, and advertisers still get what they need. The solutions are well known. OpenAI just doesn’t have the system—yet.

LOOK FOR WHAT LEADS TO RESULTS

The ad industry already turns web behavior into pseudonymized, aggregated signals about audiences and intent. OpenAI can build a stricter version of that for conversations. It already says advertisers get aggregated performance insights with no access to individual chats. Apply the same rule to intent: Roll up the commercial patterns inside conversations into categories and keep the conversations locked. We don’t need to know who said what. We need to know which kinds of needs, at which decision stage, are producing results.

This matters because of how budgets get assigned. A CMO funds a platform based on what it can prove. If ChatGPT gives me reach, impressions, and clicks with no real view of intent, I’m going to file it under experimental or awareness. The money then comes out of the innovation line or paid social. If it can connect privacy-safe intent categories to business outcomes, it gets to compete for paid search dollars, the budget set aside for capturing existing demand. That is the money pile.

MAKE INTENT MEASURABLE

Marketers have a say in which pile OpenAI gets to chase. If you want ChatGPT to become a search-caliber channel, buy it like one. Run it against paid search as well as paid social and see which it behaves like. Ask your rep what intent reporting exists today and keep asking. A click on a ChatGPT ad tells you somebody was curious. Until OpenAI shows you the intent behind it, don’t pay search prices for it.

OpenAI already has the hard part down, the thing Google spent years teaching people to do. People are telling ChatGPT their goals, problems, preferences, objections, and purchase criteria in their own words. What it hasn’t built is the advertiser’s map of all that intent.

Building it is good for the rest of us, too. When advertisers understand what people want, the ads get better. Someone who asked about an itch-free sweater under $150 should see one. That’s an ad most of us would be glad to get from a chatbot.

If OpenAI wants to be Google, it can’t hide the data for much longer. It has to make that intent measurable without making it personal.

Patrick Briggs is CEO of Semify.

#10611. How to Optimize AI-Generated Images for Faster Websites

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI-generated images are becoming a common part of modern web development. Developers use them for website banners, product illustrations, landing pages, blog posts, and digital interfaces. However, generating an image is only one part of the process. Before publishing it, developers need to ensure that the image loads quickly, displays correctly across devices, and maintains its visual quality.

Large image files can increase page size, consume unnecessary bandwidth, and delay the appearance of important content. These problems can affect user experience and website performance, particularly on mobile devices and slower internet connections.

A reliable image optimization workflow helps address these challenges. By selecting appropriate dimensions, choosing efficient image formats, automating image processing, and implementing responsive delivery, developers can improve loading performance without sacrificing visual quality.

This guide explains how to optimize AI-generated images using practical techniques and development tools.

Images often account for a significant portion of a webpage's total download size. Uploading large, unoptimized images can make pages slower and increase the amount of data visitors need to download.

Several common problems contribute to poor image performance:

Incorrect dimensions waste bandwidth on smaller screens.

Missing image dimensions can cause unexpected layout shifts.

Poor responsive configuration can make browsers download unnecessarily large images.

Incorrect loading priorities can delay important visual content.

These issues can affect Core Web Vitals, including Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), which measures how quickly the largest visible content element appears.

For developers, image optimization should therefore be part of the website development workflow rather than a final task performed immediately before publication.

Before optimizing an image, determine where it will appear on the website. A full-width banner requires different dimensions from a product thumbnail or a small interface graphic.

For example, a website might use the following dimensions:

These dimensions are examples rather than fixed requirements. The appropriate size depends on the website layout, responsive breakpoints, and supported devices.

When preparing source visuals, developers can explore different AI image generation options and consider how the generated images will fit their intended layouts.

Once the image is ready, keep a high-quality master file. This allows developers to create smaller versions for different screen sizes without repeatedly compressing an already optimized image.

Avoid enlarging small images unnecessarily because upscaling can introduce blur and visible artifacts.

Choosing the right format can reduce image size while preserving acceptable visual quality.

Three commonly used formats are AVIF, WebP, and JPEG.

AVIF: Often provides efficient compression for photographs and detailed illustrations. It can significantly reduce file sizes, although encoding may take longer.

WebP: Supports lossy and lossless compression, transparency, and animation. It offers broad browser support and is suitable for many website images.

JPEG: Remains useful for photographs and situations where compatibility with older software or systems is important.

PNG is appropriate for certain lossless graphics, screenshots, and images that require transparency. However, it can produce unnecessarily large files when used for photographic content.

No format is automatically the best choice for every image. Developers should compare file sizes and inspect visual quality before selecting the final output.

A practical approach is to generate AVIF and WebP versions and provide a JPEG fallback where necessary.

Manually resizing and converting images becomes time-consuming when a website contains dozens or hundreds of visual assets.

Automation makes the process more consistent. Developers can use Sharp, a Node.js image-processing library, to resize images, convert formats, and generate multiple versions from a single source file.

Next, create a file named build-images.mjs:

The script creates multiple image sizes in both WebP and AVIF formats.

The quality settings are starting points, not universal recommendations. Developers should adjust them after checking the resulting file sizes and visual details.

This approach is particularly useful for content-heavy websites, product catalogs, and applications that publish images regularly.

Responsive image delivery allows browsers to select an appropriate image based on the visitor's screen and the space available in the layout.

HTML provides two important attributes for this purpose: srcset and sizes.

The srcset attribute lists the available image files and their widths. The sizes attribute describes how wide the image is expected to appear at different viewport sizes.

In this example, the image is expected to occupy approximately 720 pixels on wider screens and nearly the full viewport width on smaller screens.

The browser uses this information to choose an appropriate image candidate.

One common mistake is setting sizes="100vw" for an image that occupies only a small part of the page. This can encourage the browser to download a larger file than necessary.

Always ensure that the sizes attribute reflects the actual website layout.

The HTML picture element allows developers to provide multiple image formats and a fallback option.

The browser selects a supported format, while the img element provides the fallback image and alternative text.

Developers should verify that every referenced file exists and that its dimensions match the intended layout.

The picture element can also support different crops for desktop and mobile devices. This is useful when a wide banner needs a separate composition for smaller screens.

Images without defined dimensions can cause content to move while the browser loads the file. This behavior contributes to Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS).

Including width and height attributes helps browsers reserve the appropriate space before the image finishes loading.

For responsive layouts, developers can use CSS:

This allows images to scale within their containers while maintaining their proportions.

Images below the initial viewport can generally use native lazy loading:

However, the main hero image should not normally be lazy-loaded when it is responsible for LCP. Delaying an important above-the-fold image can make the page appear slower.

Where appropriate, developers can use fetchpriority="high" for the main image to help the browser prioritize its download.

The correct strategy depends on the image's position and importance within the page.

Image optimization involves more than file size and dimensions. Developers should also consider accessibility, file organization, and metadata.

Alternative text helps people using screen readers understand meaningful images. It should describe the image's purpose in the context of the page.

Decorative images that provide no useful information should generally use an empty alt attribute.

File names should also be descriptive. Names such as home-office-sunrise.webp are easier to understand and maintain than generic names such as image-final-v3.png.

Metadata requires additional consideration. Image-processing tools may remove metadata by default to reduce file size. This can include information that a project needs to preserve, depending on its requirements.

Before removing metadata, developers should review whether the website or client requires attribution, provenance information, or other embedded details.

After implementing an optimization workflow, test the actual website rather than relying only on exported file sizes.

Chrome DevTools provides useful information about image requests.

Open Developer Tools and select the Network panel.

Resize the viewport or use device emulation.

Check whether the browser downloads appropriately sized images.

Developers can also inspect the image selected by the browser through the console:

This returns the current image URL selected for that element.

For websites with multiple images, inspect the relevant elements individually.

Finally, run an audit using Lighthouse or PageSpeed Insights. These tools can identify issues involving oversized images, image formats, loading priorities, and other performance factors.

Image optimization is only one part of website performance. Server response times, caching, CSS, JavaScript, and third-party scripts can also influence loading speed.

Several mistakes can reduce the effectiveness of an image optimization workflow:

Uploading original images without checking their dimensions.

Assuming one format always produces the smallest file.

Omitting the sizes attribute from responsive images.

Lazy-loading important above-the-fold images.

Applying excessive compression and damaging visual details.

Removing metadata without checking project requirements.

Measuring file size without inspecting the final visual quality.

A consistent testing process helps identify these issues before they affect visitors.

No. AVIF often provides efficient compression, but the results depend on the image, encoding settings, and quality requirements. Comparing both formats is the best way to choose an appropriate option.

Four to six sizes may be sufficient for many websites. The ideal number depends on the layout, responsive breakpoints, and supported devices.

Yes. Reducing the size of the main content image, providing responsive versions, and avoiding unnecessary loading delays can improve LCP when that image is the largest contentful element.

No. Lazy loading is useful for images outside the initial viewport. Important images near the top of the page should generally load promptly.

The fundamental techniques are the same as those used for conventional images. However, AI-generated visuals may contain complex textures, gradients, and fine details that require careful inspection after compression.

AI-generated images can improve website design and make it easier to create custom visual content. However, efficient delivery requires more than exporting an image and uploading it to a website.

Developers should choose suitable dimensions, compare modern image formats, automate processing, and implement responsive image delivery. Including image dimensions helps prevent layout shifts, while appropriate loading priorities can improve the experience for visitors.

By testing images across different devices and reviewing their actual performance, development teams can maintain visual quality while reducing unnecessary downloads.

A repeatable optimization workflow makes it easier to publish new visuals without sacrificing website speed, accessibility, or reliability.

#10609. How your company can become innovative

Buying new technology will not make your company innovative. It may give your people new capabilities, but technology alone will not imagine a better way to serve your customers. Only people can do that.

Artificial intelligence and automation have changed what organizations can accomplish. Challenges that once seemed too difficult or expensive are now within reach. We now know we can accomplish more, but wonder if our people are willing and empowered to imagine a better way.

At Gresham Smith, we have built our culture around the belief that innovation starts with people. Technology is a powerful tool, but people must decide where to apply it and what problem it should solve. Becoming an innovative company means building a culture where everyone feels responsible for challenging the status quo.

BUILD THE CULTURE

Here are five strategies that can help build that culture.

1. Put people before technology

Too many innovation efforts start backward. Leaders spot an impressive new technology and immediately ask how the company can use it.

Reverse the order. Start with your people and the work they do. Ask where they hit friction, which processes no longer make sense, and what they would change if old limitations disappeared. Once you understand the opportunity, then look at how technology can help.

AI and automation can make a redesigned process possible, supporting the idea, not defining it.

2. Make innovation everyone’s job

Innovation should not live in a lab or a committee. The people closest to the work usually see most clearly what needs to change.

Employees do not need “innovation” in their title to contribute. They need to understand that noticing problems and questioning assumptions are part of their jobs. They can then propose better approaches.

That message must come from leadership, consistently. People need to hear that innovation is expected. They also need to see leaders support and recognize those who act on it.

3. Create safety to challenge accepted practices

You cannot ask people to challenge the status quo and then get defensive when they do. Many established practices exist for good reasons. Others survive only because “that is how we have always done it.” Employees need the psychological safety to question both.

Leadership’s response matters most. When someone challenges an existing approach, the first reaction should be curiosity, not justification. Ask what they are seeing. Find out why the current process falls short. They question what a better outcome could look like.

Not every challenge will lead to a new solution. But shutting down questions too quickly teaches people to stop asking them.

4. Turn ideas into disciplined experiments

Psychological safety does not require you to pursue every idea. It means giving worthwhile ideas a fair shot. Build a clear path from observation to small experiment. Define the problem, name the assumption being tested, set reasonable boundaries, and decide what the team hopes to learn.

The goal of an experiment is learning, not certainty. If the results do not support the original idea, the effort was not a failure. A well-designed test can prevent a much larger investment in the wrong solution, or point the way to a better one.

5. Share what you learn

Innovation becomes part of the culture only when people can see it happening.

Tell the stories: the employee who questioned an accepted practice, tested a different approach, and applied what they learned. Celebrate the wins, but also talk about the experiments that produced useful insight without becoming permanent solutions.

These stories show employees that innovation is accessible and valued. They also help lessons travel across teams instead of staying trapped in one project or department.

Technology has opened a new world of possibility, but access to powerful tools does not automatically make an organization innovative. That takes people willing to think differently, and leaders willing to make it safe for them to do so.

Here’s a good place to start: Ask which long-standing process your people would redesign if they knew they had permission.

Mike Sewell is chief digital transformation officer at Gresham Smith.

#10606. What I had to unlearn when leaving a Fortune 500 company

For most of my corporate career, if an executive had a major speaking engagement in another country, someone from communications was getting on the plane. Often, that someone was me.

So when I moved to a startup and our CEO was invited to deliver a main-stage keynote in Paris, every instinct I’d built over more than a decade inside a Fortune 500 company told me what came next. Except this time, I didn’t get on the plane.

I worked closely on the narrative, the talk track, the slides, and coordinated with the conference team, right down to making sure his notes would appear on a downstage monitor. Then I sent him to Paris without me.

The talk was one of the strongest I’ve seen him deliver. Two years later, our team still references it and shares it with customers.

And that downstage monitor I’d carefully planned for? It wasn’t there. Something had gotten lost in translation. Fortunately, he didn’t need it.

4 THINGS I HAD TO UNLEARN

That moment captured something I’ve been learning as a leader: Becoming better can mean unlearning what doing the job well looked like.

The fundamentals I built over my career—storytelling, judgment, creativity, customer understanding, and trust—matter even more now. But some of the scaffolding around those fundamentals was built for another era. Here’s what I unlearned since.

1. Don’t rebuild the organization you left.

A startup gives you a blank canvas. That sounds freeing, until a major launch, when you notice every role that doesn’t exist. The instinct is to fill the boxes.

But I keep asking myself: If we were inventing this workflow today, would we build it the same way?

Increasingly, the answer is no.

I spent years building specialized expertise: shaping executive narratives, building thought-leadership platforms, and preparing leaders for high-stakes moments. At a startup, I’m experimenting with capturing that context in how we work, so others can use and adapt it.

The goal is to help expertise travel.

2. Don’t just make the old job faster. Redesign it.

Using AI to speed up one task is useful, but I’m more interested in what happens when teams start reimagining the work itself.

The questions I return to are simple. What context can we teach the system? Where is human judgment most important? How can someone use expertise that once lived in another person’s head?

I have a marketing team member who wanted to grow into communications. I started mentoring her on preparing executives for podcasts and speaking opportunities, and on building their social platforms. Instead of just teaching the skills, I shared how I train our brand and executive voices, so she could adapt them herself.

She went from learning to mapping out a full thought-leadership campaign on her own. After launch, an executive raved about her partnership. Soon she was building platforms for two more leaders, and bringing me ideas she’d dreamed up.

Democratizing expertise creates more builders. I’m learning to coach differently, giving others the context, tools, and confidence to build on what I know.

AI’s bigger opening is helping more people benefit from what each of us knows.

3. Speed is how fast you get it right.

Startup culture prizes speed. AI has sharpened that. Everyone expects instant answers. Recently I tested an AI workflow where the output took a few minutes. “It’s thinking,” the team said. The result was much closer to what I wanted than the usual instant response. I’d rather wait a few minutes than spend an hour prompting and rewriting.

The goal is getting it right, faster. And getting it right still requires people. That’s worth sitting with, because the pressure pulls the other way. When our team at Typeface surveyed 500+ marketing leaders, 62% admitted they’re already trading away quality, and 61% said the same about authenticity, to get cited by AI. Everyone is racing to be found. The first things to slip are the human signals that made a brand worth finding.

Being found is only the beginning. The advantage goes to brands that stay unmistakably themselves, whether they’re engaging a person or an AI agent. Human creativity is the differentiator that can’t be copied.

4. Being a strong leader doesn’t mean being in every room.

Back to Paris. I’d done the work, built the narrative, run the prep, developed the relationship. Something still went wrong, and the CEO was great.

My job was to help make sure he didn’t need me. I think about this with my team now. Sometimes an opportunity I would have owned before is better given to someone else. Sometimes expertise is more valuable when you teach it, or build it into a workflow others can use.

Scaling yourself is about creating impact in rooms you’re not in.

EXPERIENCE SHOULD GIVE YOU CONFIDENCE AND CURIOSITY

I left a Fortune 500 company for a startup expecting to be scrappy. Instead, I started questioning what we build with.

The way we work can be one thing. Context is another. The expertise of one person, captured and shared well, can serve many.

Maybe the most important one is our willingness to learn. AI is changing fast enough that none of us gets to be an expert forever. Our careers have given us judgment, pattern recognition, relationships, storytelling, and the ability to recognize great work. We also need a beginner’s mind to question the systems we’ve built around those skills.

Going first doesn’t mean adopting every new tool or discarding everything that came before. It means being willing to put your own assumptions on the table. Experience can be knowing what you’re willing to leave behind.

Courtney Brigham is senior director for communications and brand at Typeface.

#10603. How to drive social impact and business value together

Companies are often asked to drive business value while simultaneously supporting their communities. In my experience, both goals can be accomplished at the same time. We see it happening in multiple industries.

HP, for example, has connected its social impact efforts directly to its mission of helping people succeed through technology. Through its Future of Work Accelerator, the company supports nonprofits that expand access to digital tools, workforce training, and economic opportunity. The initiative helps more people develop the skills needed in today’s economy while strengthening the broader ecosystem of future workers and entrepreneurs, as well as technology users.

FedEx has taken a similar approach through its Entrepreneur Fund and Boost Camp. Small businesses make up a significant portion of the company’s customer base, and the program provides entrepreneurs with funding, mentorship, and business training to help them grow and scale their ventures. In doing so, FedEx supports local economic growth and job creation, along with small business success. At the same time, FedEx helps bolster the network of businesses that rely on its shipping and logistics services.

These efforts share a common thread: They create programs that benefit individuals and communities in need while advancing company goals.

OUR APPROACH

As NBC celebrates its 100th anniversary this year, we also have an opportunity to make a difference. We challenged ourselves to come up with an innovative way to honor our legacy while investing in the future of the creative industry.

As a media and entertainment company, our social impact efforts are naturally focused on helping the next generation of storytellers build skills, gain meaningful experience, and develop their craft.

That legacy shaped the Power of Storytelling Grants program, developed in partnership with The Alliance for Media Arts + Culture. We selected 10 emerging producers to receive $5,000 grants to create an original 30-second promotional spot honoring NBC’s centennial milestone. Each project drew from the broadcast network’s rich archive, using our iconic intellectual property to recognize our innovation, cultural moments, and industry firsts while fostering the growth of emerging creatives. One winner’s promo was selected to run across Comcast NBCUniversal platforms as part of the company’s anniversary celebration, which culminates in an on-air NBC special on December 10th.

Importantly, the grant recipients also received editorial guidance and mentorship from employee volunteers throughout the process. Access to advisors, professional networks, and real-world assignments can be the difference between aspiring to a dream job and building the key skills that will put a young creator on the path to attaining it.

The participants selected for this program were sourced from nonprofit media arts organizations, including Kids in the Spotlight, New Orleans Video Access Center, PhillyCAM, Reel Works, RE:IMAGINE, and Youth FX. These organizations are helping cultivate creative talent across the country through paid apprenticeships, and our grant program provided them with a rare opportunity for a masterclass in editing with archival footage.

INVEST IN THE NEXT GENERATION

For the winning filmmaker, Danya Granado, the experience represented more than a typical creative assignment. It was a rare moment to engage directly with a century of iconic content and cultural history. As she puts it, “The NBCU archive represents a hundred years of how people have seen news, entertainment, and each other. Getting direct access to that material feels like an invitation to be in conversation with that legacy.”

Stories like Danya’s underscore the value of capitalizing on a company’s greatest assets to invest in the next generation of talent.

Across industries, companies are creating programs that broaden access and strengthen communities. They address real societal needs while also advancing business goals. Whether it’s storytelling, technology, sports, innovation, or another core capability, every business has a superpower. The key is to use it in ways that open doors and create pathways. It should solve real challenges while also advancing strategic objectives.

Yes, it’s community impact. It’s also smart business. When done well, it’s exactly what corporate social responsibility should be: a win-win for the community and the company.

Hilary Smith is executive vice president of corporate social responsibility at NBCUniversal.

#10601. PepsiCo layoffs: 1,000 jobs reportedly slashed as CEO pushes soda giant to ‘be faster’ and ‘more capable’

November has already been a tough month for layoffs.

In the tech sector, numerous big-name companies, including Amazon, Block, and Squarespace, have already cut roles or are planning to. But workplace reductions are not limited to just tech.

Yesterday, soft drink giant PepsiCo, Inc. (Nasdaq: PEP) reportedly announced that it will lay off around 1,000 employees in North America as sales in the region underperform. Here’s what you need to know.

Pepsi tells employees to prepare for job cuts

PepsiCo CEO Ram Krishnan wrote to employees stating that the company will cut around 1,000 positions in North America in the coming days, multiple media outlets reported.

In the email Krishnan sent to employees (per CNBC), the Pepsi boss said the company’s ambitions were to “build a stronger, more future-fit business that delivers industry-leading growth” in North America.

He added: “To do that, we need to be faster, more connected, and more capable, while continuing to invest in growth — behind our people, capabilities and brands.”

Unfortunately, the endeavor also involves layoffs.

“We will simplify how we operate, better connect teams and strengthen the capabilities we need,” Krishnan wrote. “The goal is to move faster, execute better and invest behind the opportunities that will drive our growth.” The Wall Street Journal first reported the layoffs.

The layoffs will be limited to Pepsi’s North American workforce, which includes roughly 125,000 positions in the United States.

Worldwide, Pepsi employs about 306,000 people as of the end of last year. The layoffs will reportedly happen over the coming week.

Fast Company reached out to PepsiCo for comment.

Pepsi’s North American sales lag other global markets

Last month, Pepsi announced its Q3 2026 financial results, which were broadly respectable. Net revenue increased 5.6%, and operating profit increased 19%.

As CNBC reported at the time, the company’s $25.27 billion in revenue for the quarter exceeded street expectations of $24.96 billion, and its adjusted EPS of $2.34 exceeded the $2.29 analysts had expected.

But Pepsi’s relatively positive results largely came from its international markets, which, year-to-date, have accounted for 41% of its net revenue.

In Pepsi’s home territory of North America, things are less rosy.

The North American food division of Pepsi, which includes products like Frito-Lay snacks, saw volume remain flat, while its beverage business volume declined by 2%.

The lackluster results in North America led Pepsi to reduce its core earnings per share expectations for the full 2026 fiscal year. Previously, Pepsi had expected growth of 5% to 7%. Now it expects growth of 2.5% to 3.5%.

When it came to Pepsi’s North American snacks results, the company blamed the lackluster demand on “the consumer environment.”

Pepsi stock loses its fizz

Pepsi’s North American numbers are the only thing going flat. The company’s share price has lost its fizz over the course of 2026. 

PEP stock began the year performing strongly: By late February, shares were up over 20% since the year began. But since a high above $170 reached in early 2026, Pepsi shares have declined significantly. 

As of yesterday’s close, PEP stock traded at $141. While its share price has increased more than 12% over the past 30 days, that recovery has not been enough to erase the mid-year losses.

As of yesterday’s close, PEP shares were down 1.1% for the year. The broader S&P 500 is up more than 10% over that same period.

But if Pepsi executives hoped layoffs could quickly boost the company’s stock price, they’ll be disappointed. While investors tend to cheer layoffs, since cutting jobs is often the easiest way to quickly improve the bottom line, they seem to have shrugged off the news.

Since the job cuts became public yesterday, PEP shares have hardly moved. Yesterday, Pepsi stock closed up just under four-tenths of a percent, and today in premarket trading, shares are up about the same amount as of the time of this writing.

#10598. Paige Paul’s world of Dairy Boy is collabing with Hanes and coming to Target

Before the lifestyle brand Dairy Boy had a logo or a single follower, Paige Paul—formerly Paige Lorenze—was a New School student crafting a mood board made up of vlogs and pictures.

In 2021, that vision became the Dairy Boy brand—a name inspired by Paul’s love of dairy products like whole milk, which, in the age of oat milk lattes, seemed radical.

Paul, who now has an audience of more than 2.3 million across platforms, filled the brand with products that showcase pieces of her life. Her upbringing on the East Coast and the changing seasons translate into white eyelet cotton dresses in the summer and colorful fleece jackets in the winter. Then there’s the Instagram-ready pajama sets, and a sporty drop just in time for a US Open run by her husband, the American tennis player Tommy Paul. (He made it as far as the Round of 16 this year.)

“Before I had a brand, I feel like I was building a world,” Paige Paul tells Fast Company.

Now, that world of patterns and Americana lore is growing past the sold-out drops and pop-ups with hour-long lines. Dairy Boy is partnering on a limited-edition collaboration with Hanes that will sell online and at more than 1,200 Target stores nationwide beginning November 14.

Dairy Boy’s first major collaboration since it launched five years ago pairs Paul’s Americana dream with a staple of that fantasy: a brand built on comfort and functionality just like hers, but rooted in basics that were lacking in her existing collections.

“Everyone in my life, male or woman, has owned something from Hanes, and I think that is what true heritage legacy brand means in America,” Paul says. “Dairy Boy’s collections are so often vibrant and specific, and I felt like the basic side of our business is something that deserved doing it with the best in class.”

Working alongside Hanes and Target allowed Paul to keep pricing affordable. That’s a priority she traced to her days at the New School, the lower Manhattan parent of the Parsons School of Design and other colleges, when she was looking for a price point she could afford while in college.

The collection keeps the cuts, fabrics, and silhouettes of original Hanes styles, but reimages them through the lens of Dairy Boy. For instance, the collection pairs a classic white tank with men’s boxers, the first time Hanes has sold them specifically for women.

“In my first meetings with Hanes I spoke about how I always stole my husband’s boxers and wore them out to coffee or to bed, and I begged for them to allow me to use their men’s boxers, and they did,” Paul says.

The collection features 45 products, including fluffy bathrobes, waffle pants, long-sleeve sets, a triangle bralette and boy short two-packs, cami sleep dresses, and the husband-inspired boxers. On theme with the drop, small keychains in the shape of a cow wearing boxers will also be available.

While the silhouettes are classic Hanes, the patterns feature some of Dairy Boy’s most recognizable motifs, including lily of the valley, a brown bear print, camo, plaid, blue and brown pinstripe, and tartan.

The collaboration has been in the works for almost two years, as a silent project that grew alongside the brand’s own successes. Dairy Boy tripled its quarterly orders year over year, surpassing total orders from 2025 in the first nine months of 2026. And those who order seem to come back. In the third quarter of 2026, Dairy Boy reported a year-over-year increase of 312% in repeat costumer volume.

The company has grown, Paul says, thanks to its operations that resemble that of a tech company—integrating technology like AI into their back-end systems and keeping the company team lean. The startup-like structure is paired with Paul’s creative direction, which she says is driven by her gut instinct.

“I am really driving the car here, and if there is no data supporting something, but I really believe in a style, we will order it,” Paul says. “There’s no outside investment, so it’s really easy for us to make decisions quickly.”

Despite being the smaller name in the collaboration, Paul sees the Dairy Boy collection as testament to synergy, pairing the brand’s cultural pull with the infrastructure of legacy companies.

“Target has thousands of stores across America. That is something I don’t have,” she says. “The amount of people that I can get to my website for a drop is something that Target doesn’t have.”
